post1.text:
Most companies that stall between $50M and $500M don't have a strategy problem. They have a leadership problem they refuse to name.

When companies bring in senior executives specifically to handle scaling, as Buffini and Company recently did by adding three to their leadership team, they are acknowledging something most founders resist: the leader who got you to $50M is not automatically equipped to get you to $500M. That gap is real, and pretending otherwise is expensive.

Here is what scaling leaders actually need to understand:

First, your instincts that worked at $20M can actively hurt you at $100M. The speed that made you nimble now creates chaos without the right structure beneath it.

Second, leadership capacity is infrastructure. You would not scale operations without building systems. Your leadership bench deserves the same deliberate investment.

Third, the executives you hire to scale must be empowered to challenge you. Loyalty that silences honesty is a liability at this stage.

So here is the real question: Are you building a company that can outlast your current leadership style?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company added three senior executives specifically to scale their coaching business. That is a deliberate, structural move, and it signals something important.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this pattern constantly with companies growing through the $50M to $500M range. The leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who try to do more of the same. They are the ones who recognize that growth requires bringing in people who have already operated at the level you are trying to reach.

Adding executive capacity is not an admission of weakness. It is a growth strategy.

If your leadership team looks exactly the same as it did when you were half your current size, that is worth examining closely.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
When Buffini and Company added three senior executives to fuel their next stage of growth, they were doing exactly what Chapter 1 of our upcoming book addresses head on.

Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business is titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, written by Katherine Slain. It opens with a premise that makes most founders uncomfortable: the leadership identity that built your company to $50M may be the single biggest obstacle standing between you and $500M.

Katherine does not let leaders off easily in this chapter. She lays out what it actually means to lead at scale, and it goes well beyond hiring the right people. There is a specific shift in how you think, decide, and operate that has to happen first.

We are not giving that away here. But if you are running a company in growth mode, this chapter will challenge you in ways you are not expecting.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The decisions you make about who leads, how they lead, and what you are willing to change about yourself will determine whether your next phase of growth is a climb or a ceiling.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. The ones who get the best multiples start preparing years before they ever talk to a buyer.

Silicon Valley Bank recently outlined how market timing, company readiness, and owner motivation all intersect in exit decisions. The takeaway most leaders miss: readiness is not a moment, it is a posture.

If you are running a $50M+ company, here is what actually moves the needle on your valuation multiple:

1. Recurring revenue is worth more than total revenue. Buyers pay a premium for predictability, not volume.

2. Owner dependency destroys deals. If your business cannot operate without you for 90 days, your multiple suffers.

3. Clean financials are a negotiating tool. Buyers discount aggressively when they have to untangle your books during due diligence.

The companies that exit well did not get lucky. They built their businesses to be sellable long before selling was the plan.

What is the one thing in your business right now that a buyer would immediately flag as a liability?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales and private equity transactions to family succession and management buyouts.

It is a solid overview. But here is what it does not say loudly enough for scaling companies: the strategy you choose should be decided years out, not months out.

At Autobahn, we work with companies in the $50M to $500M range, and the ones who leave value on the table almost always made their exit decision reactively. The buyers with leverage are the ones sitting across from an unprepared seller.

Know your options before you need them. That is not financial planning. That is competitive strategy.

Morgan piece here and start the conversation with your leadership team now: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U

post3.text:
BDC.ca recently published research showing that a large number of business owners feel emotionally ready to exit but have done almost nothing structurally to prepare for one. The gap between intention and readiness is costing owners real money.

This is exactly the problem that Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, was written to solve.

The chapter is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman. One thing they make clear early: your valuation multiple is not determined at the negotiating table. It is determined by decisions you made two, three, or five years before you ever sat down with a buyer.

Most owners do not know which levers actually move their multiple. Chapter 2 names them specifically.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because leadership teams never built a system to execute it.

Forbes recently explored why execution breaks down at the leadership level, and the pattern is familiar: smart people, solid ideas, and no repeatable process to bring them to life.

Here is what scaling companies need to hear:

1. Strategy without a cadence is just a document. If your team is not reviewing progress on a fixed rhythm, the plan is already dead.

2. Accountability has to be specific. Who owns what, by when, and what does success look like? Vague ownership produces vague results.

3. The gap between planning and execution is usually a people alignment problem, not a strategy problem. Your leadership team needs to agree on priorities before anyone leaves the room.

Companies between $50M and $500M are especially vulnerable here. The complexity has outgrown informal coordination, but the systems have not caught up.

What is the single biggest execution breakdown you see in your organization right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Harvard Business School Online does a solid job breaking down what separates companies that implement strategy well from those that simply plan well. The distinction matters more than most leaders admit.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and the execution gap is almost always the bottleneck. Leadership alignment, clear ownership, and a structured review process are not nice-to-haves at that stage. They are the difference between compounding growth and stalled momentum.

The companies that scale fastest treat execution as a discipline, not an afterthought to the annual planning retreat.

If your team is better at building plans than running them, this article is worth fifteen minutes of your time.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiZ0FVX3lxTE5pcmMwWURjZ3NNYXZQOUI4V1Vwalk4TTJORHlsOEZOM2FlZG9ZSmw1LWFGc0RIYzNOcFNZbTkxRFhjWjdTdWkzek04UEhLblBJdWVUaGg2ZEsyeHJKd01YTXV6QXpTb2M

Strategic planning sounds sophisticated. Execution is where things get humbling.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on real experience running very different businesses to show why most execution problems start long before anyone tries to implement anything.

The insight that sticks: the planning process itself is where execution is won or lost. By the time your team leaves the room, the conditions for success or failure are already set.

It is a lesson that applies whether you are moving product off shelves or managing a $200M services firm.

If you are leading a company that has outgrown its current planning approach, this chapter will make you rethink where you spend your time before the work begins.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think they have a sales strategy. What they actually have is a revenue habit.

There is a difference. A habit is what your team does when no one is watching. A strategy is what your team does when the market shifts and customers stop coming to you.

Recent research from McKinsey confirms what we see constantly with scaling companies: the threshold for sustainable B2B growth has risen sharply. What worked to get you to $50M is actively working against you at $150M.

Here is what that means in practice:

First, your top three reps should not be carrying institutional knowledge that lives nowhere else in the business. That is a liability, not an asset.

Second, if your sales process is not documented and repeatable, you are not scaling sales. You are scaling dependency.

Third, pricing strategy and sales strategy are the same conversation. Separating them is how margin quietly disappears.

So ask yourself honestly: if your two best salespeople left tomorrow, would your revenue strategy survive the week?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain and Company breaks down what actually separates B2B growth winners from companies that plateau. The findings are worth sitting with: top performers are not just selling more, they are selling differently, with sharper segmentation, cleaner go-to-market motions, and a ruthless focus on customer retention as a growth lever.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. The ones who stall are usually not losing on product. They are losing on structure. Their sales approach was built for a smaller business and nobody stopped to redesign it.

If your growth has started to feel harder than it should, your sales strategy deserves a serious look before your pipeline does.

Read the Bain piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMijwFBVV95cUxQaER1TkZ6Z1pHUk54TXNYOTJ1SlllM2EzWkVLSEpVQklOOFl4OXc5V3gwdEowdlFOUmx5V3lJc0hZQ3pjWWswNzZrQ1BsSnJ1c1VYV1k5SXpkU1Z6Z1ZrNFVxUFNzQUM3OFQyX0JsOVRHY3IyeFFyOXhNakJoTkgxQV9qQjRWSlVHNXprN1lDQQ?oc=5

post3.text:
New research from McKinsey and Bain is pointing to a hard truth for B2B companies: the bar for real growth has gotten higher, and most sales strategies were not built to clear it.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business tackles this head-on. The chapter is called Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, written by Deb and Brandon, and the title is not a metaphor. It is math.

One thing they make clear early: there is a difference between having salespeople and having a sales system. Most companies at $50M have the former and believe they have the latter. That gap is expensive, and it compounds quietly until growth stops feeling like growth.

If you are building toward $500M, this chapter will change how you look at every deal in your pipeline.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have no idea what that feeling actually is.

Adweek recently covered how Campari manages a portfolio of iconic brands by anchoring each one to a distinct cultural identity rather than just a product story. That discipline is rare, and it is exactly what separates companies that scale from companies that plateau.

Here is what mid-market leaders consistently get wrong about branding:

1. They confuse marketing activity with brand clarity. More campaigns do not fix a fuzzy identity.
2. They build for customers they have, not customers they want at $500M.
3. They let the brand drift as they add products, geographies, and teams, with no one accountable for consistency.

Ulta's CMO recently talked about blending brand building with omnichannel execution. That only works when the brand itself is airtight first.

So here is the real question: If your best customer had to describe your company in one sentence, would you be proud of what they said?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Adweek broke down how Campari preserves the cultural identity of its iconic brands while still keeping them relevant and commercially aggressive. It is a masterclass in what most scaling companies ignore entirely.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Companies growing from $50M toward $500M invest heavily in sales infrastructure and operations, then wonder why revenue stalls. The answer is often sitting in the brand. When your identity is unclear internally, it becomes invisible externally.

Campari's approach works because leadership treats brand as a business asset, not a marketing department project. That mindset shift changes everything.

If you are scaling and your brand still feels like an afterthought, that is the problem worth solving first.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxOME5NSGZueEQtNEplYmN2bWt2NHBnYWlPNEM3Wm5JYnhlMzNxSGpiRkxhN1NmVVh2UnVFa0dXTG1rNFA3d05RdkRNcUkxcGlaMVRSTklhZDFpVkttRVN1SFFGY2lVRDRncTQ3WXQwYkx3NW55MHdiTGlYVlN0ZXBJa0NtYjVCa21FOFF6eFNFYVZPcVFyTk91OG5rZ2FRX1M0MnNvalZFQW1PVXBUZDJIcmFaSlMtUFJkVFZz?oc=5

post3.text:
Ulta's CMO recently talked about the challenge of building a brand that holds together across every channel and every customer touchpoint simultaneously. It sounds simple. It is not.

Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' and authored by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, confronts exactly this problem for companies in the $50M to $500M growth window.

The chapter opens with a provocation most leaders are not ready for: your customers already have a perception of your brand, whether you shaped it or not. Simpson and West lay out a framework for getting honest about what your marketing is actually communicating, not just what you intend it to say.

The gap between those two things is where growth gets stuck.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

It is whether your customers feel something consistent every time they encounter you, and whether that feeling is one you deliberately built. Here is what scaling companies get wrong about brand, and how to fix it before it costs you the next hundred million.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a liability strategy.

Most companies scaling past $50M treat talent acquisition like a volume game. Post more roles, interview more candidates, fill more seats. SHRM recently reported that the new standard for hiring in 2026 is precision over scale, meaning the highest-performing organizations are getting more intentional about fewer, better hires rather than running headcount up and hoping output follows.

Here is what that actually means for a mid-market business leader:

First, your cost-per-bad-hire compounds. One wrong VP of Sales does not cost you a salary. It costs you 18 months of pipeline.

Second, your hiring process is a signal. Candidates are evaluating your organization the moment they hit your job description. Sloppy process communicates sloppy culture.

Third, speed without criteria is just expensive chaos. Defining what great looks like before you post is not optional at this stage of growth.

So here is the real question: Are you building a talent engine, or just keeping up with turnover?

post2.text:
A recent piece in UC Today made a point that every scaling company should sit with: your HR platform does not fix bad hiring decisions. It just moves them faster and further across your organization.

That is a real problem for companies in the $50M to $500M range. At that stage, you are adding systems, adding headcount, and adding complexity all at once. If your talent criteria are weak going in, automation and integration will not save you. They will just make the mistakes harder to trace and more expensive to unwind.

At Autobahn, we see this consistently. Technology is not the talent strategy. It is the tool that executes the strategy. Getting that order right is what separates companies that scale cleanly from ones that scale painfully.

Read the full piece and think honestly about what your platform is actually multiplying: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxQWjRQeU5RQWw1SlRfNElDUmhDVDFNUDBXeTE1NlJUOVI2TmVTVGY0aVpTVDJXYlh2bm1OWXhFUkFVZFZQT2tfWDQxMFowcm5jWWRLWlpPNFp5bUJyMXlhdnR5NkxXWTBVWGFzTDVDaGVNYnZEVjRxSEVSQW9jVmZzbGVyTjYwSzZBUTd0LWtvWWlyOEk5Qmg5bEduaHRuVTNTdUhqVDhETGFtZw?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring is not new to us. It is exactly what Chapter 6 of our upcoming book addresses head-on.

In The Talent Engine, authors Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West lay out what it actually takes to build a people strategy that holds up as your company scales from $50M toward $500M and beyond. The chapter does not start with recruiting tools or org charts. It starts with something most leadership teams skip entirely: defining what the right person looks like before the pressure to fill a role takes over.

That one shift changes everything downstream. Hiring, onboarding, retention, performance. All of it.

If your talent process feels reactive right now, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better leaders. They make distracted ones.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter and call it accountability. Harvard Business School research backs this up, showing that organizations often track marketing performance data they never actually use to make decisions. The dashboard grows. Clarity shrinks.

Here is what high-growth leadership teams do differently:

1. They pick fewer metrics and defend that list aggressively. Five meaningful numbers beat thirty decorative ones every time.

2. They tie every KPI to a decision. If a metric cannot change what you do next week, it has no place in your review.

3. They review KPIs on a cadence that matches the speed of the business, not the speed of the spreadsheet.

Scaling from $50M to $500M requires operational precision, not operational noise. The companies that get there are not measuring more. They are measuring what matters.

What is one metric your leadership team tracks that nobody has ever acted on?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounded up 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs. Solid resource. But here is what the article does not say.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, the tool is rarely the problem. The problem is that leadership teams have not agreed on which numbers actually represent the health of the business. You can plug the best software in the world into a broken measurement strategy and get beautifully formatted noise.

At Autobahn, we work with scaling companies to cut through that noise. Before you evaluate another platform, get clear on who owns each metric, how often it gets reviewed, and what action it is supposed to drive.

Tool selection comes last, not first.

Read the full article here and then ask your team whether your process is actually ready for it: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Every fast-growing company eventually hits the same wall. The metrics multiply, the meetings get longer, and somehow decisions get harder.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is called Death by KPIs for a reason. Authors Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall wrote it because they have watched otherwise excellent leadership teams suffocate under the weight of their own dashboards.

One of the core ideas in that chapter: the number of KPIs a company tracks often goes up as accountability goes down. More measurement becomes a substitute for more clarity.

If your team spends more time building reports than acting on them, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most executives are measuring AI wrong, and it is costing them real money.

A global study by TCS found that 84% of executives rank productivity as AI's top benefit. That sounds like a win. But here is the problem: productivity gains on their own do not scale a business. They just make a stalled machine run faster.

If you are leading a company between $50M and $500M, here is what actually matters:

1. AI should be eliminating decision bottlenecks, not just speeding up tasks. If your leadership team is still the chokepoint, you have a structure problem, not a software problem.

2. The companies pulling ahead are not adopting more AI tools. They are going deeper with fewer, purpose-built into their workflows.

3. ROI from AI is lagging for most organizations because adoption is happening without process redesign. Technology without operational clarity is just expensive noise.

Productivity is a byproduct of intelligent systems. It is not the goal.

What is your company actually optimizing for when it invests in AI?

post2.text:
A recent piece in IT Brief Asia caught our attention. Singapore CEOs are reporting real productivity gains from AI, but return on investment is still lagging behind expectations.

This pattern is not unique to Singapore. We see it constantly with scaling companies in the $50M to $500M range.

Here is the gap: leaders are deploying AI at the task level without redesigning the systems around it. You cannot bolt new technology onto an outdated operating structure and expect financial results to follow.

Productivity without process alignment is just activity. And activity is not growth.

If your AI investments are not connecting to measurable business outcomes yet, the issue is almost never the technology. It is the architecture around it.

Read the full article here and think about where your own ROI gap lives: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihwFBVV95cUxNYnhGcHlxUHVhQVk1b3pqWHJMbjFnNlFvUEx3NWdPRzNwby1jMzNXNlZpVGlTZjVySGlCeExFMjh2VXhGVU95eTBwekhtMTVjSE9ZRmlWdVd0MWh1cEtxTlpzTmFROGtpNTZac0FnbmNGLTJPaEZGX2RuN19KaHUwdG5LeEE0SGM

post3.text:
84% of executives say AI's top benefit is productivity. So why are so many companies struggling to show real ROI from their AI investments?

Chapter 8 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this directly. The chapter is called The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it reframes how scaling companies should think about AI integration entirely.

The insight is not about which tools you use. It is about where AI sits inside your decision-making structure. Most organizations are adding AI to the edge of their operations. The companies that scale fast are placing it at the center.

There is a specific way to do that without creating chaos in your leadership team, and Chapter 8 lays out exactly how.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Global executives are sold on AI's ability to boost productivity. But for companies scaling past $50M, productivity is not the prize. The real question is whether your AI investments are built into the structure of how decisions get made, or just layered on top of work that was already happening. post1.text:
The leaders who feel most confident are often the most dangerous ones in the room.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a problem to fix. It is not. It is a signal that you are operating at the edge of your competence, which is exactly where growth happens. A recent Campaign US piece made this case directly: stop trying to eliminate the feeling and start learning to use it.

For leaders scaling companies past $50M, here is what that actually looks like in practice:

First, imposter syndrome sharpens your listening. You ask better questions when you do not assume you have all the answers. That is a competitive advantage, not a weakness.

Second, it creates intellectual honesty. Leaders who feel settled in their expertise stop stress-testing their assumptions. That is when blind spots become fatal.

Third, the feeling often spikes right before a breakthrough. It is not evidence that you do not belong. It is evidence that the stakes have gotten real.

So here is the question worth sitting with: What decision are you avoiding right now because imposter syndrome is whispering that you are not ready?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US challenged the conventional wisdom around imposter syndrome, arguing that leaders should stop trying to outgrow it and start putting it to work instead.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and beyond, this reframe matters more than most leadership teams realize. At that stage, you are constantly making decisions with incomplete information, entering markets you have never played in, and hiring people who know things you do not. The discomfort is structural. It is not going away.

The leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who feel confident. They are the ones who have learned to act decisively while still feeling uncertain.

If your leadership team is treating self-doubt as a liability rather than a tool, that is worth examining. Read the full article here and see what comes up for you.

post3.text:
Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it asks a question most high-growth leaders quietly carry but rarely say out loud.

Written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, the chapter goes directly at the leadership psychology that shows up when companies are scaling fast and the stakes are higher than anything the leader has faced before.

One of the most useful things it surfaces: imposter syndrome does not disappear as your company grows. For many leaders, it intensifies. And the way you respond to it at $50M will shape whether you are still the right person in the seat at $500M.

The chapter does not offer a cure. It offers something more practical than that.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every leader who has scaled a company past $50M knows the feeling: success that does not quite feel earned, decisions made with more confidence than certainty, and a quiet voice asking whether this is the moment it all falls apart. Imposter syndrome is not a sign that you are in the wrong seat. It may be the clearest sign that you are in exactly the right one.

post1.text:
The most dangerous thing a $50M+ founder can do is optimize their business without ever optimizing their life.

Most leaders at this stage treat personal planning as a reward for later. Something to figure out after the next milestone, the next raise, the next exit. But research consistently shows that founders who sell their businesses often experience profound regret within the first year, not because the deal was bad, but because they never defined what they actually wanted beyond the company.

Here is what high-growth leaders rarely hear:

First, your business plan and your life plan need the same rigor. Vague personal goals produce the same results as vague business goals.

Second, the $500M version of your company may require a version of you that you have not yet designed. That gap has real operational consequences.

Third, 'work-life balance' is the wrong frame entirely. The better question is whether your work is funding a life you have intentionally chosen.

What does success actually look like for you outside the building?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur reported that three out of four founders regret selling their business within a year of closing the deal. The number is striking, but the reason behind it is what matters: most of them had no clear vision of what life after the business was supposed to look like.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern well before the exit. Leaders scaling from $50M toward $500M pour enormous energy into revenue strategy, team structure, and market expansion. Very few apply that same discipline to their own life design.

If you do not know what you are building toward personally, every business decision becomes a guess. Clarity at the life level creates better decisions at the company level.

Read the full article here and ask yourself: do you have a plan for what comes next?

post3.text:
Three out of four founders regret selling within a year. That statistic is not a cautionary tale about deal structure. It is a warning about what happens when leaders never stop to design the life they are actually working toward.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, addresses exactly this. Written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter gives scaling leaders a framework for integrating life planning into their growth strategy, not as an afterthought, but as a core operating discipline.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter: the executives who struggle most after a major business transition are rarely the ones who failed at business. They are the ones who never got clear on what they wanted outside of it.

There is a process for getting that clarity. We will share more soon.

The same rigor you apply to revenue targets, team design, and market positioning belongs in your personal planning too. Here is why that work cannot wait until after the exit.
